summary.text: Writing the coefficient as \(3^n\prod_{t=0}^{n-1}(9t+2)(9t+4)(9t+6)(9t+7)/((3n)!n!)\), the proof shows prime-by-prime that the denominator divides the numerator: for \(p\ne3\), Legendre’s formula reduces this to counting the four relevant residue classes modulo each \(p^i\), with an explicit analysis of the six classes coprime to \(9\). For \(p=3\), each factor \(9t+6\) supplies one power of \(3\), and together with the prefactor \(3^n\) this dominates \(v_3((3n)!n!)=n+2v_3(n!)\), since \(2v_3(n!)\le n\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
F(x)={}_3F_2\!\left(\frac29,\frac49,\frac79;\frac13,1;729x\right)
     =\sum_{n\ge 0}a_nx^n.
\]
We prove that every coefficient \(a_n\) is an integer.

Recall that, with \((u)_n=u(u+1)\cdots(u+n-1)\),
\[
a_n=729^n\frac{(2/9)_n(4/9)_n(7/9)_n}{(1/3)_n(1)_n n!}.
\]
Since \((1)_n=n!\), the quotient of two successive coefficients is, for \(n\ge1\),
\[
\frac{a_n}{a_{n-1}}
 =729\frac{(n-1+2/9)(n-1+4/9)(n-1+7/9)}{(n-1+1/3)n^2}
 =\frac{3(9n-7)(9n-5)(9n-2)}{n^2(3n-2)}.
\]
Also \(a_0=1\).

We will use a different closed form. Define
\[
P_n=\prod_{t=0}^{n-1}(9t+2)(9t+4)(9t+6)(9t+7),
\]
with the empty product equal to \(1\), and put
\[
N_n=3^nP_n,\qquad D_n=(3n)!\,n!.
\]
We first check that
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle a_n=\frac{N_n}{D_n}.} \tag{1}
\]
Indeed, both sides equal \(1\) for \(n=0\). Moreover,
\[
\frac{N_n/D_n}{N_{n-1}/D_{n-1}}
 =\frac{3(9n-7)(9n-5)(9n-3)(9n-2)}{(3n-2)(3n-1)(3n)n}.
\]
Using \(9n-3=3(3n-1)\) and \(3n\cdot n=3n^2\), this simplifies to
\[
\frac{3(9n-7)(9n-5)(9n-2)}{n^2(3n-2)},
\]
which is exactly the recurrence ratio for \(a_n\). Thus (1) follows by induction.

It remains to prove
\[
D_n\mid N_n. \tag{2}
\]
We prove this prime by prime.

For a prime \(p\), write \(v_p(M)\) for the exponent of \(p\) in a positive integer \(M\). We shall use the standard formulas
\[
v_p(M!)=\sum_{i\ge1}\left\lfloor\frac{M}{p^i}\right\rfloor,
\qquad
v_p(u)=\sum_{i\ge1}\mathbf 1_{p^i\mid u}. \tag{3}
\]
All these sums are actually finite.

The principal counting lemma
--------------------------------

We need the following inequality. If \(q>1\) and \(\gcd(q,9)=1\), then for every \(n\ge0\),
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{3n}{q}\right\rfloor+
\left\lfloor\frac n q\right\rfloor
\le
\sum_{t=0}^{n-1}\sum_{d\in\{2,4,6,7\}}
 \mathbf 1_{q\mid 9t+d}. \tag{4}
\]

We now prove (4) completely. Since \(9\) is invertible modulo \(q\), for each fixed \(d\) the condition \(q\mid9t+d\) selects one residue class of \(t\pmod q\). Write
\[
n=kq+s,\qquad 0\le s<q.
\]
If the selected residue has representative \(r\), \(0\le r<q\), then among \(t=0,1,\ldots,n-1\) its number of occurrences is
\[
k+\mathbf 1_{r<s}. \tag{5}
\]
Furthermore,
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{3n}{q}\right\rfloor
=3k+\left\lfloor\frac{3s}{q}\right\rfloor.
\]
Consequently, after the common contribution \(4k\) is removed, (4) is equivalent to
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{3s}{q}\right\rfloor
\le \#\{d\in\{2,4,6,7\}:r_d<s\}, \tag{6}
\]
where \(r_d\) is the representative solving \(9r_d+d\equiv0\pmod q\). The four residues are counted with multiplicity; this matters if two displayed representatives happen to coincide.

Because \(q\) is coprime to \(9\), its residue modulo \(9\) is one of
\(1,2,4,5,7,8\). Write \(q=9m+c\). Direct substitution gives the following representatives, all lying in \([0,q)\):
\[
\begin{array}{c|cccc|cc}
 c&r_2&r_4&r_6&r_7&\text{smallest}&\text{second smallest}\\ \hline
1&2m&4m&6m&7m&2m&4m\\
2&m&2m&3m&8m+1&m&2m\\
4&5m+2&m&6m+2&4m+1&m&4m+1\\
5&4m+2&8m+4&3m+1&5m+2&3m+1&4m+2\\
7&8m+6&7m+5&6m+4&m&m&6m+4\\
8&7m+6&5m+4&3m+2&2m+1&2m+1&3m+2
\end{array} \tag{7}
\]
For example, in the first row
\(9(2m)+2=2q\), \(9(4m)+4=4q\), and similarly for the other entries. In the second row the corresponding identities are
\[
9m+2=q,
\quad9(2m)+4=2q,
\quad9(3m)+6=3q,
\quad9(8m+1)+7=8q,
\]
and direct expansion proves every remaining entry in the table. The inequalities \(0\le r_d<q\) are immediate from the displayed formulas. In the case \(c=1\), the assumptions \(q>1\) and \(q=9m+1\) imply \(m\ge1\), which is the only minor endpoint issue.

Since \(0\le s<q\), the left side of (6) can only be \(0,1\), or \(2\). It is at least \(1\) exactly when \(3s\ge q\), and it is \(2\) exactly when \(3s\ge2q\). Thus it suffices to check:

* if \(3s\ge q\), the smallest residue in the row is less than \(s\);
* if \(3s\ge2q\), the two smallest residues in the row are both less than \(s\).

These checks are short integer inequalities. We record them row by row so that all cases are explicit.

* If \(q=9m+1\), then \(m\ge1\). From \(3s\ge q\) one gets \(s\ge3m+1>2m\). From \(3s\ge2q\) one gets \(s\ge6m+1>4m\).
* If \(q=9m+2\), then \(3s\ge q\) gives \(s\ge3m+1>m\), while \(3s\ge2q\) gives \(s\ge6m+2>2m\).
* If \(q=9m+4\), then \(3s\ge q\) gives \(s\ge3m+2>m\), while \(3s\ge2q\) gives \(s\ge6m+3>4m+1\).
* If \(q=9m+5\), then \(3s\ge q\) gives \(s\ge3m+2>3m+1\), while \(3s\ge2q\) gives \(s\ge6m+4>4m+2\).
* If \(q=9m+7\), then \(3s\ge q\) gives \(s\ge3m+3>m\), while \(3s\ge2q\) gives \(s\ge6m+5>6m+4\).
* If \(q=9m+8\), then \(3s\ge q\) gives \(s\ge3m+3>2m+1\), while \(3s\ge2q\) gives \(s\ge6m+6>3m+2\).

Thus (6), and hence the counting inequality (4), holds in every possible residue class of \(q\).

Prime valuations away from \(3\)
----------------------------------

Let \(p\ne3\) be prime. For every \(i\ge1\), the prime power \(q=p^i\) satisfies \(q>1\) and \(\gcd(q,9)=1\). Applying (4) with \(q=p^i\) gives
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{3n}{p^i}\right\rfloor+
\left\lfloor\frac n{p^i}\right\rfloor
\le
\sum_{t=0}^{n-1}\sum_{d\in\{2,4,6,7\}}
 \mathbf 1_{p^i\mid9t+d}.
\]
Sum this inequality over \(i\ge1\). By (3), the left side becomes
\[
v_p((3n)!)+v_p(n!)=v_p(D_n).
\]
On the right, we may interchange the finite sums. Again by (3), it becomes
\[
\sum_{t=0}^{n-1}\sum_{d\in\{2,4,6,7\}}v_p(9t+d)
=v_p(P_n).
\]
Since \(p\ne3\), we have \(v_p(3^n)=0\), and therefore
\[
v_p(D_n)\le v_p(P_n)=v_p(N_n). \tag{8}
\]

The exceptional prime \(3\)
----------------------------

We next prove the same inequality for \(p=3\). First,
\[
v_3((3n)!)=n+v_3(n!). \tag{9}
\]
Indeed, among \(1,2,\ldots,3n\), the multiples of \(3\) are precisely
\(3,6,\ldots,3n\). They contribute one factor of \(3\) each, and after those factors are removed their remaining product is \(n!\). The numbers not divisible by \(3\) contribute nothing to the \(3\)-adic valuation.

Let \(f=v_3(n!)\). By Legendre's formula,
\[
f=\sum_{i\ge1}\left\lfloor\frac n{3^i}\right\rfloor
\le \sum_{i\ge1}\frac n{3^i}=\frac n2.
\]
Thus
\[
2f\le n. \tag{10}
\]

For every \(t\), the factor \(9t+6=3(3t+2)\) is divisible by \(3\). Hence each of the \(n\) terms in the product defining \(P_n\) supplies at least one factor of \(3\), so
\[
v_3(P_n)\ge n. \tag{11}
\]
Using (9)--(11),
\[
\begin{aligned}
v_3(D_n)
 &=v_3((3n)!)+v_3(n!)\\
 &=n+2f\\
 &\le n+v_3(P_n)\\
 &=v_3(3^nP_n)=v_3(N_n).
\end{aligned} \tag{12}
\]

Completion of the divisibility argument
-----------------------------------------

Equations (8) and (12) show that for every prime \(p\),
\[
v_p(D_n)\le v_p(N_n).
\]
Both \(D_n\) and \(N_n\) are positive integers. By unique prime factorization, the displayed inequalities for all primes are equivalent to
\(D_n\mid N_n\). This proves (2).

Finally, (1) gives
\[
a_n=\frac{N_n}{D_n}.
\]
Since \(D_n\mid N_n\), this quotient is an integer. Therefore every coefficient of
\[
{}_3F_2\!\left(\frac29,\frac49,\frac79;\frac13,1;729x\right)
\]
is an integer, as claimed.
